subject: MGMT160
title: What Managers Do: Functions, Roles, Skills and Levels

questions.stem: Describe management, using the definition in the chapter.
options: Planning, organising, leading and controlling resources to reach goals effectively and efficiently
Giving instructions to staff and checking that every order is carried out exactly as it was given by the manager
Holding the most senior, best-paid position and representing the firm to outsiders
Doing the technical work faster and to a higher standard than anyone else on the team
questions.why: The definition has four functions (P-O-L-C) and two tests (effective and efficient). Orders, offices and status are not in it. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Identify the test the chapter uses to decide if a person is a manager.
options: The person coordinates the work of others and is judged by the team's results
The person has the word 'manager' in the job title and a reserved parking space
The person earns more than the people around them and has a private office
The person has worked in the firm longer than anyone else in the department
questions.why: Title, pay and seniority do not make a manager; coordinating others' work and being judged on the team's results does. See §1.2 and the answer to question 4 in §1.7.

questions.stem: Explain the meaning of effectiveness.
options: Doing the right things — the activities that achieve the goal
Doing things right — getting the most output from the least input
Finishing every task faster than the nearest competitor can
Spending the least possible money on every activity in the business
questions.why: Effectiveness = doing the RIGHT things (the goal is reached). Efficiency = doing things RIGHT (least waste). See §1.3 The Two Magic Words.

questions.stem: Explain the meaning of efficiency.
options: Getting the most output from the least input
Choosing the right goal for the business and pursuing it consistently
Making every customer happy whatever it costs the business
Having the largest and most experienced team in the market
questions.why: Efficiency is about input and output — doing things right with little waste. Air Arabia is the chapter's example. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Identify the four functions of management in the correct order.
options: Planning, organising, leading, controlling
Leading, planning, controlling, organising
Organising, controlling, planning, leading
Planning, leading, hiring, controlling
questions.why: P-O-L-C: plan what to achieve, organise who does what, lead and motivate people, control by checking results. Fayol, 1916. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Describe the organising function.
options: Deciding who will do what, with which resources
Deciding what the business should achieve and how it will get there
Motivating, guiding and communicating with people so they do the work well
Checking whether goals are being achieved and fixing what has gone wrong
questions.why: Organising = structure, job responsibilities and resources: who cooks, who serves, who orders supplies. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Describe the controlling function.
options: Monitoring performance, comparing it to the goal and fixing problems
Giving staff strict rules and clear punishments so that mistakes are not repeated
Setting measurable goals and deadlines for the year
Hiring, training and dismissing employees according to the needs of the business
questions.why: Controlling means watching results against the goal and fixing the cause — the strong manager asks WHY when complaints rise. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify the three families of managerial roles described by Mintzberg.
options: Interpersonal, informational, decisional
Technical, human, conceptual
Top, middle, frontline
Planning, organising, leading and controlling
questions.why: Mintzberg's three families: interpersonal (people), informational (information), decisional (decisions). Skills and levels are different lists. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Describe what Mintzberg found when he followed real managers with a stopwatch.
options: Half of their activities took less than nine minutes, with constant interruptions
They spent most of the day alone in the office, writing detailed plans for the year ahead
They gave orders for most of the day and rarely spoke to anyone outside their own team
They spent most of the day in long, scheduled meetings with other senior managers
questions.why: Managerial work is juggling, not chess: short tasks, constant switching. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Identify the role family that includes the monitor, disseminator and spokesperson roles.
options: Informational
Interpersonal
Decisional
Conceptual
questions.why: Monitor (collect), disseminator (tell the team), spokesperson (speak for the team) are the informational roles — 'the team's radar and voice'. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Identify the level of management that thinks in years and makes the big bets.
options: Top managers
Middle managers
Frontline managers
Team members
questions.why: Top managers (CEO, board) set direction and think in years; middle in months; frontline in days. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Describe the main job of middle managers.
options: Turning the top managers' direction into budgets, teams and timelines
Deciding whether the company should expand into a new country or a new product line
Making the daily staff schedule and solving the problems that come up on the shift
Doing the specialised technical work themselves to a higher standard than the team
questions.why: Middle managers (branch managers, department heads) turn 'expand' into budgets, teams and timelines, thinking in months. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Identify the three managerial skills in Katz's skills triangle.
options: Technical, human, conceptual
Planning, leading, controlling
Interpersonal, informational, decisional
Speaking, writing, computing
questions.why: Katz: technical (job knowledge), human (working with people), conceptual (big-picture thinking). See §1.8.

questions.stem: Identify the skill that matters at every level of management, always.
options: Human skills
Technical skills
Conceptual skills
People skills
questions.why: Human skills are critical at every level because management IS people. Technical is heaviest at the frontline, conceptual at the top. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Describe the evidence the chapter gives that managers matter.
options: Gallup found the direct manager explains about 70% of the difference in team engagement
A survey found that most managers in large companies now hold an MBA or equivalent degree
Managers earn on average about 70% more than the members of the teams they lead
Companies that employ more managers per employee grow faster than their competitors
questions.why: Gallup (2015): the direct manager explains about 70% of the difference in team engagement. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Determine the correct description of a café that makes good coffee at low cost but keeps losing customers.
options: Efficient but not effective
Effective but not efficient
Both effective and efficient
Neither effective nor efficient
questions.why: Low cost = efficient (doing things right). Losing customers = not effective (the goal is not reached). See the 2×2 table in §1.3.

questions.stem: Classify a student who studies twelve hours the night before the exam and performs badly.
options: Neither efficient nor effective
Efficient but not effective
Effective but not efficient
Both efficient and effective at once
questions.why: Huge input, small output (not efficient); the goal — a good grade — not reached (not effective). See the answer to question 3 in §1.3.

questions.stem: Identify the management function a café owner is using when she writes the goal '120 covers a day by June'.
options: Planning
Organising
Leading
Controlling
questions.why: A goal with numbers and a date is planning — 'be popular' is a wish; '120 covers a day by June' is a plan. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Identify the management function a manager is using when complaints rise and he compares the numbers to the goal and fixes the cause.
options: Controlling
Planning
Organising
Leading
questions.why: Monitoring results against the goal and fixing the cause is controlling. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a group project where 'everyone did everything' and the work was late. Determine the most likely management failure.
options: An organising failure — nobody was given a clear role
A leading failure — the team was not motivated to finish the work on time
A controlling failure — nobody checked progress against the deadline each week
A planning failure — the group never agreed on a goal for the project
questions.why: When everyone does everything, roles were never assigned. The chapter's mini-question says this is usually an organising failure. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Classify the role when Amna briefs her team on this weekend's promotion.
options: Informational — disseminator
Interpersonal — figurehead
Decisional — negotiator
Decisional — resource allocator
questions.why: Telling the team what it needs to know is the disseminator role in the informational family. See One Hour with Amna, 9:20, §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify the role when a supplier calls to say the delivery is three days late and Amna negotiates a partial delivery tomorrow.
options: Decisional — negotiator and disturbance handler
Informational — monitor, disseminator and spokesperson
Interpersonal — liaison and figurehead
Interpersonal — leader and liaison
questions.why: Handling a surprise and negotiating a solution are decisional roles. See Amna at 9:30, §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify the role when Amna moves one person from the stockroom to the shop floor for the weekend rush.
options: Decisional — resource allocator
Informational — spokesperson
Interpersonal — figurehead
Informational — disseminator of news
questions.why: Dividing people, money and time between tasks is the resource allocator role (decisional). See Amna at 9:55, §1.6.

questions.stem: Classify the role when Amna notices a team member looks exhausted and takes five minutes to check on him.
options: Interpersonal — leader
Decisional — disturbance handler
Informational — monitor
Decisional — entrepreneur
questions.why: Motivating and caring for people is the leader role in the interpersonal family. See Amna at 9:45, §1.6.

questions.stem: Determine the level of management of a person who decides whether the company should open in Saudi Arabia next year.
options: Top management
Middle management
Frontline management
Not a manager
questions.why: Direction and big bets, thinking in years, belong to top managers. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Determine the level of management of a night-shift nursing supervisor who makes the schedule and coaches her nurses.
options: Frontline management
Top management
Middle management
Not a manager — an expert
questions.why: Schedules, problems and coaching, thinking in days, are frontline management. See the hospital column in §1.7.

questions.stem: Compare a senior surgeon with no team and a head of nursing for one floor. Determine which one is a manager.
options: Only the head of nursing — she coordinates others and is judged by the team's results
Only the surgeon — he is more senior, more qualified and earns more than she does
Both — they are senior hospital staff with responsibility for patients' outcomes and for the hospital's reputation
Neither — the chapter says managers are found only in business organisations
questions.why: The test is coordinating others' work, not seniority or salary. The surgeon with no team is an expert, not a manager. See the answer to question 4, §1.7.

questions.stem: Analyse why a brilliant cook who is promoted to restaurant manager often struggles in the new job.
options: Promotion rewarded technical skill, but the manager's job runs on human and conceptual skills
Cooking skill becomes useless once you are a manager, so the kitchen no longer respects the cook
Managers only need conceptual skills, which cooks never have the chance to develop
The cook was not senior enough to be promoted, so the older staff refuse to follow instructions
questions.why: Katz's puzzle: promotion rewards technical skill, but the job needs human and conceptual skills nobody tested. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Select the skill mix the chapter defends for a hospital manager.
options: Conceptual 40 · Human 40 · Technical 20
Technical 60 · Human 20 · Conceptual 20
Human 50 · Technical 25 · Conceptual 25
Technical 40 · Conceptual 40 · Human 20
questions.why: A hospital is a system of systems; the manager need not be a doctor, so technical is lightest. See the table in §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse the two cafés with the same products, prices and customers where one succeeds and one closes. Determine the most likely reason.
options: The quality of management decisions made about the same resources
One café had more money behind it and could survive the slow months
One café had better coffee beans and a more experienced barista
Customers prefer new cafés and move on when the novelty wears off
questions.why: Both cafés had the same resources; the difference was the quality of the decisions made about them. Talent without direction pulls in different directions. See the answer to questions 1 and 2 in §1.1.

questions.stem: Explain why two cafés with the same products and prices can have different results.
options: The quality of management decisions about the same resources is different
One café always has better luck with its location, its suppliers and its customers
Customers prefer the older café because they are used to it
The bigger café always wins because it can buy supplies more cheaply
questions.why: Same resources, different decisions. Management is what turns talent and money into results. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Describe what the Gallup study says about the direct manager.
options: The direct manager explains about 70% of the difference in team engagement
The direct manager decides the company's prices and therefore its profits
The direct manager explains about 10% of engagement; pay explains the rest
Managers have no measurable effect on engagement once pay is taken into account
questions.why: Gallup (2015): about 70% of the variation in engagement comes from the manager. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Explain the chapter's claim that talent without direction is wasted.
options: Talented people pull in different directions unless a manager gives them one goal
Talented people never need a manager because they can set their own goals and keep to them
Direction only matters in small firms where everybody knows each other
Talent always finds its own direction if it is given enough time and freedom
questions.why: Without management, talented people work hard but not together. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Identify the two tests inside the chapter's definition of management.
options: Effective and efficient
Fast and cheap
Big and famous
Strict but friendly at the same time
questions.why: Management achieves goals effectively (right things) and efficiently (least waste). See §1.2.

questions.stem: Describe the difference between a manager and an expert.
options: A manager coordinates the work of others; an expert does the work personally
A manager works longer hours than an expert and carries more responsibility
An expert earns more than a manager because specialist knowledge is scarce
There is no real difference; the two titles are used for the same job in most firms
questions.why: Coordinating others' work is the test; doing the work yourself makes you an expert. See §1.2.

questions.stem: Describe a business that is effective but not efficient.
options: It reaches its goal but wastes a lot of input to get there
It reaches its goal with the least possible input and no waste
It fails to reach its goal although it uses its resources carefully
It fails to reach its goal
questions.why: Effective = goal reached; not efficient = high waste. See the 2×2 table in §1.3.

questions.stem: Identify the chapter's example of an efficient airline.
options: Air Arabia
Emirates
Etihad
flydubai
questions.why: Air Arabia is the chapter's example of efficiency — most output from least input. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Describe the leading function.
options: Motivating, guiding and communicating with people so they do the work well
Writing the yearly budget and allocating the money between the departments of the business
Checking the results against the plan and correcting what has gone wrong
Deciding who reports to whom and which resources each team will use
questions.why: Leading = people: motivate, guide, communicate. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Describe the decisional family of roles.
options: Entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator
Figurehead, leader, liaison, spokesperson
Monitor, disseminator, spokesperson, liaison and figurehead
Planner, organiser, leader, controller
questions.why: Decisional roles are about making choices: start things, fix surprises, divide resources, negotiate. See §1.5.

questions.stem: Describe the main job of frontline managers.
options: Running the daily work: schedules, problems and coaching, thinking in days
Setting the company's direction for the next five years and making the big bets
Turning strategy into budgets, teams and timelines, thinking in months
Owning the company and appointing the people who will run it
questions.why: Frontline managers think in days. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Identify the three levels of management.
options: Top, middle, frontline
Owner, employee, customer
Owner, staff, customer
Senior, junior, trainee
questions.why: Top (years), middle (months), frontline (days). See §1.7.

questions.stem: Describe conceptual skills.
options: Seeing the big picture and how the parts of the organisation fit together
Knowing how to do the technical work of the department to a high standard
Getting on well with people and understanding what motivates them
Using software and data confidently to prepare reports and budgets
questions.why: Conceptual = big-picture thinking, heaviest at the top. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Identify the skill that is heaviest at the frontline level.
options: Technical skills
Conceptual skills
Negotiation skills
Financial skills
questions.why: Frontline managers need the most technical skill; conceptual grows with level. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a team of talented people who all work hard but the project is still late. Determine the most likely cause.
options: Nobody gave the team one direction — talent without management
The team was not talented enough
The team worked too few hours and underestimated the work involved
The project was too easy, so the team lost interest and stopped trying
questions.why: Talent without direction pulls in different directions. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's answer to 'do managers really matter?'.
options: Yes — the direct manager explains about 70% of the difference in engagement
No — only the quality of the product decides how engaged a team is in the long run
Only in very large companies where staff rarely meet the senior leaders
Only when salaries are low and the manager is the main reason to stay
questions.why: Gallup's 70% finding is the chapter's evidence. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Select the best evidence that management, not resources, decides results.
options: Two cafés with identical resources where one succeeds and one closes
A rich company that grows faster than its smaller competitors because it has more money
A café that wins customers because it buys better coffee beans
A company whose famous logo brings customers in without advertising
questions.why: Same resources, different results — the difference is management. See §1.1.

questions.stem: Classify a delivery company that delivers every parcel on time but spends twice the budget on fuel.
options: Effective but not efficient
Efficient but not effective
Both effective and efficient
Neither effective nor efficient
questions.why: Goal reached (effective) with waste (not efficient). See §1.3.

questions.stem: Classify a student who studies little, spends no money on books, and still gets a high grade.
options: Both efficient and effective
Efficient but not effective
Effective but not efficient
Neither effective nor efficient
questions.why: Least input, goal reached. See §1.3.

questions.stem: Determine the management function used when a shop owner decides that Sara runs the till and Omar handles stock.
options: Organising
Planning
Leading
Controlling
questions.why: Deciding who does what is organising. See §1.4.

questions.stem: Determine the level of a department head who turns the CEO's growth target into this year's budget and team plan.
options: Middle management
Top management
Frontline management
Not a manager
questions.why: Middle managers turn direction into budgets, teams and timelines. See §1.7.

questions.stem: Select the skill mix the chapter would expect for a frontline kitchen supervisor.
options: Technical heavy, human high, conceptual light
Conceptual heavy, human high, technical light
Equal thirds of technical, human and conceptual
Human only, with no technical or conceptual skill needed
questions.why: At the frontline technical skill is heaviest; human skill is always high. See §1.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a new manager who knows the work perfectly but her team is unhappy and quitting. Determine the missing skill.
options: Human skills
Technical skills
Conceptual skills
IT skills
questions.why: Management IS people; human skills matter at every level. See §1.8.
